nationality_or_literary_tradition: American; short-story writer and novelist writing in English
literary_identity: American short-story writer of the Georgia backcountry, a Roman Catholic whose comic and violent stories of the action of grace - 'A Good Man Is Hard to Find', 'Good Country People' - are among the most admired in the language
biography: Mary Flannery O'Connor was born in Savannah, Georgia, on 25 March 1925, the only child of Edward Francis O'Connor and Regina Cline; the family moved to Milledgeville in 1940, her father died of lupus in 1941, and she took her degree at Georgia State College for Women in 1945 and studied at the Iowa Writers' Workshop, where she took her MFA in 1947. She wrote Wise Blood (1952) and The Violent Bear It Away (1960), the stories of A Good Man Is Hard to Find and Other Stories (1955) and Everything That Rises Must Converge (1965, posthumous), the essays and lectures of Mystery and Manners (1969) and the letters of The Habit of Being (1979). In 1950 she was diagnosed with disseminated lupus, the disease that had killed her father, and lived for the rest of her life at her mother's farm at Andalusia, near Milledgeville, raising peacocks and writing in the mornings; she died on 3 August 1964, at 39, and The Complete Stories won the National Book Award in 1972.
literary_profile: Novels: Wise Blood (1952) and The Violent Bear It Away (1960). Stories: A Good Man Is Hard to Find and Other Stories (1955), Everything That Rises Must Converge (1965) and The Complete Stories (1971). Non-fiction: Mystery and Manners: Occasional Prose (1969) and The Habit of Being: Letters (1979), with the early stories in The Geranium: A Collection of Short Stories (1975).
stylistic_characteristics: A comic, exact and mercilessly flat style in which grotesque events are reported without comment; dialogue that reproduces the idiom of the rural South with great precision; a habit of ending a story with a single turn that reverses everything before it; violent imagery used as the instrument of revelation rather than of sensation.
intellectual_concerns: Grace and the resistance to it, in explicitly Catholic terms; sin, redemption and judgement; the grotesque body and the disabled body; race and the American South in the years of desegregation; mothers and daughters, and the family as a field of violence; the pretensions of the educated and the secular.
historical_significance: O'Connor is one of the great American short-story writers of the century and the central figure of the Southern Gothic after Faulkner; her stories are standard anthology texts, The Complete Stories won the National Book Award, and her essays on the writing of fiction, collected in Mystery and Manners, are among the most cited by American writers on craft.
bibliographical_notes: The titles and dates above come from Wikipedia's article on O'Connor and from its pages on the individual stories, read directly; they were not checked against a printed bibliography. Installment 10 records only the three Norton selections - 'Good Country People' (Harper's Bazaar, June 1955), 'A Good Man Is Hard to Find' (Modern Writing I, 1953) and 'Everything That Rises Must Converge' (New World Writing, October 1961) - so the two novels, the other stories and the letters have no records and the bibliography is incomplete.

nationality_or_literary_tradition: American; poet, essayist and activist writing in English
literary_identity: American poet of the Beat Generation whose long breath-lines and candour about sexuality, madness and empire made 'Howl' the founding poem of the postwar American counterculture
biography: Irwin Allen Ginsberg was born in Newark, New Jersey, on 3 June 1926, the son of Louis Ginsberg, a poet and high-school teacher, and Naomi Levy Ginsberg, whose mental illness and early death marked his life and his work. He entered Columbia University in 1943, met Jack Kerouac, William Burroughs and Neal Cassady there, was suspended and later arrested in connection with a stolen car, spent eight months in a psychiatric institute in 1949 at his own request, and moved to San Francisco in 1954, where he read 'Howl' at the Six Gallery in October 1955 and saw it published by City Lights in 1956. Howl and Other Poems was the subject of an obscenity trial in 1957, which it won; Kaddish and Other Poems (1961), Reality Sandwiches (1963), Planet News (1968), The Fall of America (1972, National Book Award), Mind Breaths (1977), Plutonian Ode (1982), White Shroud (1986) and Cosmopolitan Greetings (1994) followed, with the essays of Deliberate Prose and the photographs and songs. He was a public figure of the anti-war and gay liberation movements, studied with Buddhist teachers from the 1970s, and died in New York on 5 April 1997.
literary_profile: Poetry: Howl and Other Poems (1956), Kaddish and Other Poems (1961), Reality Sandwiches (1963), Planet News (1968), The Fall of America (1972), Mind Breaths (1977), Plutonian Ode (1982), White Shroud (1986), Cosmopolitan Greetings (1994) and Death and Fame (1999), with Collected Poems 1947-1997 (2006). Prose: Deliberate Prose: Selected Essays (2000), Journals: Mid-Fifties (1995) and the letters with Kerouac and Cassady.
stylistic_characteristics: The long breath-line: a line measured by the length of a single exhalation rather than by the foot, with parataxis in place of subordinate clauses; catalogues of people and things; a diction that mixes the prophetic, the obscene and the documentary; repetition and incantation derived from Hebrew liturgy and from jazz.
intellectual_concerns: Madness, confinement and the destruction of the gifted by American society; sexuality and the closet; war, empire and the military-industrial state; the sacred in the ordinary and in the body; friendship and the Beat community; Buddhism, chant and the discipline of attention; testimony, and the poet as witness.
historical_significance: Ginsberg is the most public poet of the American postwar avant-garde and 'Howl' the poem through which the Beat Generation is defined; the 1957 obscenity trial became a landmark of American free expression, the poem is a standard anthology and course text, and Ginsberg's readings, recordings and activism made him one of the best-known poets of the century.
bibliographical_notes: The biography and the list of books above come from Wikipedia's article on Ginsberg and on 'Howl', read directly; they were not checked against a printed bibliography. Installment 10 records only the Norton selection, 'Howl' (written 1954-55; Howl and Other Poems, City Lights, 1956); the other collections, the essays and the journals have no records, so the bibliography is incomplete.

nationality_or_literary_tradition: American; novelist and short-story writer writing in English
literary_identity: American novelist and theorist of the exhausted mode, the most programmatic of the American postmodernists, whose Lost in the Funhouse (1968) turned the short story into an essay on its own making
biography: John Simmons Barth was born in Cambridge, Maryland, on 27 May 1930, the son of a candy-store owner; he studied briefly at the Juilliard School, took his BA and MA at Johns Hopkins University, and taught at Pennsylvania State University from 1953 to 1965 and then at the State University of New York at Buffalo, before returning to Johns Hopkins in 1973 as Alumni Centennial Professor, retiring in 1995. The Floating Opera (1956) and The End of the Road (1958) are realist novels, The Sot-Weed Factor (1960) and Giles Goat-Boy (1966) mock-epic ones; Lost in the Funhouse (1968) followed his essay 'The Literature of Exhaustion' (1967) and made him the leading theorist of American metafiction, and Chimera (1972) won the National Book Award in 1973. LETTERS (1979), Sabbatical (1982), The Tidewater Tales (1987), The Last Voyage of Somebody the Sailor (1991), Once Upon a Time (1994) and Coming Soon!!! (2001) followed, with the non-fiction of The Friday Book (1984) and Further Fridays (1995). He died at Bonita Springs, Florida, on 2 April 2024.
literary_profile: Novels: The Floating Opera (1956), The End of the Road (1958), The Sot-Weed Factor (1960), Giles Goat-Boy (1966), Chimera (1972), LETTERS (1979), Sabbatical (1982), The Tidewater Tales (1987), The Last Voyage of Somebody the Sailor (1991), Once Upon a Time (1994), Coming Soon!!! (2001) and Every Third Thought (2015). Stories: Lost in the Funhouse (1968), On with the Story (1996) and The Development (2008). Non-fiction: The Friday Book (1984) and Further Fridays (1995).
stylistic_characteristics: Stories that interrupt themselves to discuss their own construction, with footnotes, diagrams, blank pages and alternative endings; pastiche of earlier genres from the eighteenth-century novel to the detective story; a prose of great rhetorical energy and comic pedantry; the repeated figure of the author as a character in his own text.
intellectual_concerns: The exhaustion of literary forms and the possibility of writing after them; storytelling as a subject in itself; myth, epic and the oldest stories reused; identity as performance and as quotation; the artist's career and the relation of a writer to his own earlier books; the comic and the cosmic.
historical_significance: Barth is the figure through which American postmodernism and metafiction are usually taught, and 'The Literature of Exhaustion' is one of the most cited critical essays of the postwar decades; Lost in the Funhouse is a standard text in courses on the American short story and on experimental fiction, and his influence on the writers who followed him - from Barth's own students to the metafiction of the 1970s and 1980s - is widely acknowledged.
bibliographical_notes: The titles and dates above come from Wikipedia's articles on Barth and on Lost in the Funhouse, read directly; they were not checked against a printed bibliography. Installment 10 records only the Norton selections of the title story, 'Lost in the Funhouse' (The Atlantic Monthly, November 1967; collected 1968); the novels, the other stories and the criticism have no records, so the bibliography is incomplete.

nationality_or_literary_tradition: American; essayist, novelist and screenwriter writing in English
literary_identity: American essayist and novelist whose cool, fragmentary reports on California and on American politics - Slouching Towards Bethlehem, The White Album - made her the most imitated prose stylist of American non-fiction
biography: Joan Didion was born in Sacramento, California, on 5 December 1934, into a family of California pioneers; she took her degree in English at the University of California, Berkeley, in 1956, won a Prize from Vogue for an essay and worked at the magazine in New York for eight years, and married the writer John Gregory Dunne in 1964, with whom she wrote screenplays and adopted a daughter, Quintana. Run River (1963) was her first novel; Slouching Towards Bethlehem (1968) made her reputation as an essayist, and Play It As It Lays (1970), A Book of Common Prayer (1977), Democracy (1984) and The Last Thing He Wanted (1996) are the later novels. The White Album (1979) collected the essays of the 1970s, followed by Salvador (1983), Miami (1987), After Henry (1992), Political Fictions (2001) and Where I Was From (2003); The Year of Magical Thinking (2005), written after Dunne's death in 2003, won the National Book Award, and Blue Nights (2011) followed the death of her daughter. She died in New York on 23 December 2021.
literary_profile: Non-fiction: Slouching Towards Bethlehem (1968), The White Album (1979), Salvador (1983), Miami (1987), After Henry (1992), Political Fictions (2001), Where I Was From (2003), The Year of Magical Thinking (2005), We Tell Ourselves Stories in Order to Live (2006) and Blue Nights (2011). Novels: Run River (1963), Play It As It Lays (1970), A Book of Common Prayer (1977), Democracy (1984) and The Last Thing He Wanted (1996). Screenplays, with John Gregory Dunne, include Panic in Needle Park (1971) and A Star Is Born (1976).
stylistic_characteristics: Short declarative sentences and a deliberately flat rhythm; the repeated phrase and the returning motif as structure; juxtaposition of reportage and private recollection without transition; quotation of documents, testimony and song lyrics; a first person that is present but withheld, and an irony that never quite becomes judgement.
intellectual_concerns: California as a place and a state of mind; the 1960s and their aftermath, above all in Los Angeles; narrative itself and the stories people tell to survive; women's lives and the pressure of feminine roles; politics, media and the manipulation of images; grief, illness and memory.
historical_significance: Didion is the most influential American essayist of the last half-century and the model for the personal, reportorial non-fiction that followed her; The White Album was named by Publishers Weekly among the ten most important essays since 1950, The Year of Magical Thinking won the National Book Award, and her sentences are among the most quoted in modern American prose.
